q-33322.name: Question 1
q-33322.problem: Find an equation of the plane that contains the point  $Q(5,2,3)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n=6i+5j+4k.$
q-33322.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of $Q$ is $q=5i+2j+3k$ and $n=6i+5j+4k$ is normal to the plane. 

The equation of the plane that passes though the point $Q({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n$ can be given as

$$
(r-q)\cdot n=0,
$$

where $r$ is the position vector of any point on the plane, and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-q)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-q\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =q\cdot n \\ r\cdot (6i+5j+4k) & =(5i+2j+3k)\cdot (6i+5j+4k) \\ r\cdot (6i+5j+4k) & =52.\end{aligned}
$$

q-127645.problem: Find an equation of the plane that contains the point $P(3,-2,4)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n=⟨1,-2,-1⟩.$
q-127645.worked_solution:
First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨3,-2,4⟩,$ and $n=⟨1,-2,-1⟩$ is normal to the plane.

The equation of the plane that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n$ can be given as

$$
(r-p)\cdot n=0,
$$

where $r$ is the position vector of any point on the plane, and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨1,-2,-1⟩ & =⟨3,-2,4⟩\cdot ⟨1,-2,-1⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨1,-2,-1⟩ & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we note that the position vector of P is p=⟨3,−2,4⟩, and n=⟨1,−2,−1⟩ is normal to the plane.

The equation of the plane that passes through the point P(x0,y0,z0) and is perpendicular to the vector n can be given as (r−p)⋅n=0, where r is the position vector of any point on the plane, and p is the position vector of P.

So, we have (r−p)⋅n=0r⋅n−p⋅n=0r⋅n=p⋅nr⋅⟨1,−2,−1⟩=⟨3,−2,4⟩⋅⟨1,−2,−1⟩r⋅⟨1,−2,−1⟩=3.

q-33027.problem: Find an equation of the plane that contains the point $Q(1,2,-1)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
q-33027.worked_solution:
First, note that the position vector of $Q$ is $q=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ and $n=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ is normal to the plane.

The equation of the plane that passes though the point $Q({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n$ can be given as

$$
(r-q)\cdot n=0,
$$

where $r$ is the position vector of any point on the plane, and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-q)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-q\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =q\cdot n \\ r\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ r\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, note that the position vector of Q is q=[12−1] and n=[2−43] is normal to the plane.

The equation of the plane that passes though the point Q(x0,y0,z0) and is perpendicular to the vector n can be given as (r−q)⋅n=0, where r is the position vector of any point on the plane, and q is the position vector of Q.

So, we have (r−q)⋅n=0r⋅n−q⋅n=0r⋅n=q⋅nr⋅[2−43]=[12−1]⋅[2−43]r⋅[2−43]=−9.

q-33035.problem: Find an equation of the plane that contains the point  $P(1,-\sqrt{3},4)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n=8i+\sqrt{27}j.$
q-33035.worked_solution:
First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=i-\sqrt{3}j+4k$ and $n=8i+\sqrt{27}j$ is normal to the plane.

The equation of the plane that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n$ can be given as 

$$
(r-p)\cdot n=0,
$$

where $r$ is the position vector of any point on the plane, and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot (8i+\sqrt{27}j) & =(i-\sqrt{3}j+4k)\cdot (8i+\sqrt{27}j) \\ r\cdot (8i+\sqrt{27}j) & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-32972.problem: Find an equation of the plane that contains the point $Q(5,-1,1)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n=⟨-1,-2,3⟩.$
q-32972.worked_solution:
First, we note that the position vector of $Q$ is $q=⟨5,-1,1⟩$ and $n=⟨-1,-2,3⟩$ is normal to the plane.

The equation of the plane that passes though the point $Q({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n$ can be given as

$$
(r-q)\cdot n=0,
$$

where $r$ is the position vector of any point on the plane, and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-q)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-q\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =q\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-1,-2,3⟩ & =⟨5,-1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-1,-2,3⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-1,-2,3⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Submit

EXPLANATION

The equation of the plane that passes though the point Q(x0,y0,z0) and is perpendicular to the vector n can be given as (r−q)⋅n=0, where r is the position vector of any point on the plane, and q is the position vector of Q.

q-70822.name: Question 6
q-70822.problem: A nonzero vector $⟨a,\,b,\,0⟩$ is parallel to the plane $r\cdot ⟨-5,-1,4⟩=6.$ What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
q-70822.worked_solution:
We need a vector $v=⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩$ that is parallel to the given plane. 

From the equation $r\cdot ⟨-5,-1,4⟩=6$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨-5,-1,4⟩.$ So, $v⊥n$ and we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨-5,-1,4⟩ & =0 \\ -5{t}_{1}-{t}_{2}+4{t}_{3} & =0 \\ {t}_{2} & =-5{t}_{1}+4{t}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain 

$$
v=⟨{t}_{1},-5{t}_{1}+4{t}_{3},{t}_{3}⟩,
$$

where ${t}_{1},{t}_{3}\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

We are told that the third component of $v$ equals $0.$ So, we must set ${t}_{3}=0.$ 

Since $v$ is nonzero, we can pick any ${t}_{1}\ne 0.$ For example, setting ${t}_{1}=1$, we get

$$
v=⟨1,\,-5,\,0⟩.
$$

We need a vector v=⟨t1,t2,t3⟩ that is parallel to the given plane.

From the equation r⋅⟨−5,−1,4⟩=6 of the plane, we get the normal vector n=⟨−5,−1,4⟩. So, v⊥n and we have the following:

v⋅n=0⟨t1,t2,t3⟩⋅⟨−5,−1,4⟩=0−5t1−t2+4t3=0t2=−5t1+4t3

Hence, we obtain v=⟨t1,−5t1+4t3,t3⟩, where t1,t3∈(−∞,∞).

We are told that the third component of v equals 0. So, we must set t3=0.

Since v is nonzero, we can pick any t1≠0. For example, setting t1=1, we get

v=⟨1,−5,0⟩.

Therefore, ab=−15.

q-127910.problem: A nonzero vector $⟨a,\,0,\,c⟩$ is parallel to the plane $r\cdot ⟨-1,1,3⟩=\sqrt{7}.$ What is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$
q-127910.worked_solution:
We need a vector $v=⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩$ that is parallel to the given plane. 

From the equation $r\cdot ⟨-1,1,3⟩=\sqrt{7}$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨-1,1,3⟩.$ So, $v⊥n$ and we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,1,3⟩ & =0 \\ -{t}_{1}+{t}_{2}+3{t}_{3} & =0 \\ {t}_{1} & ={t}_{2}+3{t}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain 

$$
v=⟨{t}_{2}+3{t}_{3},\,{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩,
$$

where ${t}_{2},{t}_{3}\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

We are told that the second component of $v$ equals $0.$ So, we must set ${t}_{2}=0.$ 

Since $v$ is nonzero, we can pick any ${t}_{3}\ne 0.$ For example, setting ${t}_{3}=1$, we get

$$
v=⟨3,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Therefore, $\frac{a}{c}=3.$
